title: John 1:1, where Jesus is 'a god'
claim: The New World Translation reads 'and the Word was a god' at John 1:1. Nearly every major English Bible reads 'the Word was God' — the KJV, NIV, ESV, NASB, NRSV, and the Catholic NAB. Bruce Metzger of Princeton called the rendering 'a frightful mistranslation,' and also 'erroneous,' 'pernicious' and 'reprehensible' (Theology Today, April 1953). The wording serves the Watchtower's denial that Christ is God. But it creates a problem their own theology cannot absorb. If the Word is 'a god' alongside Jehovah, their Bible now teaches a second, lesser god. Yet in that same Bible Jehovah says: 'before me there was no God formed, and after me there continued to be none' (NWT Isaiah 43:10). Watchtower literature defends the reading by pointing to the missing Greek definite article before theos, and to a handful of obscure translations. It also collides with John's own habit. The word theos stands without the article in John 1:6, 12, 13 and 18, and there the NWT prints 'God.'

He argues that a predicate theos without the article is grammatically indefinite or qualitative. So 'a god' or 'divine' is a defensible rendering, and 'the Word was God' actually over-translates the Greek. Colwell's Rule, long cited against the NWT, is not a real rule of Greek grammar requiring definiteness. Even Daniel Wallace concedes that conservative scholars misapplied it. Philip Harner's 1973 study in the Journal of Biblical Literature showed the construction is mainly qualitative: the Word has God's nature. The Watchtower says its rendering keeps that sense without collapsing the Word into the Father, whom John distinguishes in the same verse ('the Word was with God').

title: 'Other' added four times, then the brackets vanished
claim: In Colossians 1:16-17, and again in verse 20, the NWT inserts the word 'other' — 'by means of him all other things were created... he is before all other things.' The Greek words for 'other,' allos and heteros, appear nowhere in these verses in any manuscript. Paul's point is that Christ created all things, full stop. Inserting 'other' turns the passage into evidence that Christ is himself a created thing who then made everything else. That is precisely Watchtower doctrine. The editorial history is damning. The 1950 edition printed 'other' with no brackets. After criticism, later editions bracketed it, 'all [other] things,' marking it as an addition. The 2013 revision removed the brackets again, so current readers cannot see that the word is not in the Greek. The same move is not made at Romans 8:38-39 or John 1:3, where 'all things' is left alone. The insertion appears exactly where Christology is at stake.

title: Hebrews 1:8, where Westcott agreed with them
claim: Hebrews 1:8 quotes Psalm 45:6. It is traditionally rendered 'But of the Son he says, Your throne, O God, is forever and ever' — the Father addressing the Son as God. The NWT reads 'God is your throne forever and ever,' which removes the address. Critics have long listed this among the NWT's doctrinally motivated changes, since the chapter argues for the Son's superiority to angels, and a vocative reading makes verse 8 its climax. The Greek, ho theos, is formally ambiguous between vocative and nominative. So the question is whether the NWT's choice is a defensible option or special pleading. The NWT makes the same move in the psalm itself, at Psalm 45:6. Notably, verse 10 goes on to apply Psalm 102 — words addressed to YHWH about creating heaven and earth — directly to the Son, and the NWT translates that straightforwardly.

title: Luke 23:43, where everything hangs on a comma
claim: To the thief on the cross, Jesus says, in all major translations, 'Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise.' The NWT moves the comma: 'Truly I tell you today, you will be with me in paradise.' Jesus is merely saying it today, and promising paradise at some unspecified later point. The relocation protects two Watchtower doctrines at once: soul sleep, since the thief cannot be conscious anywhere that day, and a two-class afterlife, since the thief belongs to the earthly-paradise class rather than to heaven. The pattern evidence is strong. Forms of 'truly I say to you' occur over 70 times in the Gospels, and in no other instance does a time adverb attach to the saying formula rather than to the content. The earliest manuscripts, however, carry virtually no punctuation, so the comma is an editorial decision in every translation. The question is whose decision follows the evidence and whose follows doctrine.

response: The earliest Greek manuscripts had no punctuation, so no translation can claim manuscript authority for its comma. Codex Vaticanus actually has a point after semeron, 'today.' The Curetonian Syriac, from the 5th century, explicitly reads 'Truly I say to you today, that with me you will be...' Hesychius of Jerusalem, who died about 434, attests that some readers punctuated exactly as the NWT does, so this is an ancient reading rather than a Watchtower invention. Rotherham's Emphasized Bible punctuates the same way. 'I tell you this day' is a solemn Hebrew declaration idiom, as in Deuteronomy 30:18, and natural on the lips of a dying Jewish teacher. And Jesus himself was not in paradise that day; he was in the grave until the third day (Acts 10:40).

responseSource.name: NWT Defended — History of the Comma at Luke 23:43

rationale: The NWT's rendering is doctrinally motivated, but it has genuinely ancient attestation in the Curetonian Syriac and in Hesychius' report, and the point about manuscript punctuation is simply true. Against it stand the 70-plus occurrences of the amen formula, never elsewhere modified by 'today,' and the emptiness of Jesus solemnly noting that he is speaking 'today' to a man dying beside him. Most textual scholars side with the traditional comma, but this is a probability judgment, not a proof. Grade it contested. Use it to illustrate how doctrine steers supposedly neutral decisions, rather than as a standalone charge of mistranslation.

plain.d: Jesus speaks to the thief dying beside him. Most Bibles read: "Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise." Their Bible moves the comma: "Truly I tell you today, you will be with me in paradise." Now Jesus is only noting the day he is speaking.

It guards two teachings at once. Witnesses teach that the dead know nothing, so the thief could not be conscious that day. They also teach two futures: heaven for a few, earth for the rest. The thief belongs to the earthly group.

The oldest Greek copies carry almost no punctuation. So no Bible can claim manuscript backing for its comma. Codex Vaticanus has a point after the word for "today." The Curetonian Syriac, from the 400s, reads it their way. Hesychius of Jerusalem, who died about 434, reports readers who punctuated like this. Rotherham's Emphasized Bible does the same. "I tell you this day" is also a solemn Hebrew way of speaking (Deuteronomy 30:18). And Jesus was in the grave until the third day (Acts 10:40).

title: 1,500 died in the camps: don't dismiss it
claim: 'They're just a cult — there's nothing to respect about them.' It is used to wave away the movement wholesale, usually as a preface to an argument about 1914 or blood.
response: This one is not merely rude. It is false, and a Witness knows the history far better than the person using it. Under the Third Reich, Jehovah's Witnesses were the only group persecuted purely for a religious position they could have ended at any moment by signing a renunciation. Roughly 10,000 were imprisoned. Around 1,500 died. About 250 were executed for refusing military service. They wore the purple triangle in the camps, and the survivor literature, including accounts from Jewish survivors, repeatedly describes them as the prisoners least likely to inform and most likely to share food. In the United States they litigated their way to the Supreme Court more than fifty times between 1938 and 1955, and the case law they won belongs to everyone. West Virginia v. Barnette (1943) established that no American can be compelled to salute a flag or profess a belief. Cantwell v. Connecticut (1940) applied the Free Exercise Clause to the states. Much of the religious-liberty protection every American church now relies on was bought by Jehovah's Witnesses in court. Russia banned the organization as extremist in 2017 and has imprisoned members since, so the persecution is not only historical.
